The autopilot system receives its instructions from the command element. The Omni/Heading Switch selects which command source to use, Manual or Navigational.
When the command source is set to Heading (HDG), commands to the autopilot are read from the control panel of the autopilot. When the command source is set to omni, commands are read from VOR system.
Computing Systems are used to manipulate and address received data. Some autopilot systems do not use computers, they send sensing and command signals to an amplifier then to the output elements.
The Omni/Heading Switch tells the autopilot what mode of operation to use. The Heading Mode (HDG) follows the information set by the autopilot control panel like heading, turn and pitch.
The Altitude Hold Switch tells the autopilot to hold the plane at a current altitude. This control is either ON or OFF.
The Master Switch turns the autopilot ON and OFF. If a malfunction occurs a manual switch is used to disengage the autopilot.

Some autopilot systems are more complex and require a computer to manipulate the data it receives. For example, an autopilot that was designed to land a plane needs a computer to perform all of the steps required for a proper landing sequence.

Slats help to decrease the stall speed of the plane. One functional difference between the slot and slat is that the slat is adjustable and the plain slot is normally fixed.

A rudder trim tab is normally located on the bottom edge of the rudder. This trim tab can be adjusted by a wheel or crank when the aircraft is on the ground or in the air. The purpose of the rudder trim tab is to relieve pressure on the cockpit rudder pedals.

When landing, flaps reduce the landing speed shortening the length of landing rollout. This makes landing in small or obstructed areas possible because it allows the glide angle to increase without greatly increasing approach speed.
Slots are placed on the leading edge of the wing. Slots allow smooth air flow across the wing.

Slats are movable surfaces which are connected to the front or leading edge of a wing. When the slat is closed it forms the leading edge of the wing. When open it creates a slot in the leading edge of the wing.

When these plates are used to slow the plane down and decrease the lift they are known as speed brakes. There is a separate control in the cockpit for using these plates as speed brakes. In this mode of operation all plates are deflected upward.

There is also another type of tail assembly known as a ruddervator. This system replaces the rudder, elevator and stabilator three surface design with a two surface design in the shape of a V.

The rudder is located at the tail end of the plane and is attached to a vertical stabilizer, also known as a fin. The rudder is used to maneuver the plane on the yaw axis. The rudder is controlled by two foot pedals in the cockpit.
When the left pedal is depressed the rudder moves left. This causes the nose of the plane to move left and the tail to move right.

Elevator trim tabs are normally located on the inner edge of the tail stabilizers. Just as with the aileron trim tabs, these tabs relieve pressure on the elevators. These trim tabs can be adjusted while the aircraft is on the ground or in the air by a crank or wheel adjustment depending on the type of plane.

Elevators are mounted on a stabilizer. A stabilizer is a small stationary wing located at the tail end of the plane. The stabilizer is stationary while the elevators move to change the pitch of the plane. When the yoke is pulled back the elevators move up. When the yoke is pushed forward the elevators are moved down.

A stabilator is a small wing located at the tail end of the plane that moves up and down to change the pitch of the plane. The entire stabilator moves up and down, not just a portion of it like the elevators.

When the aileron moves upward, the push-rod moves, which causes the spring to move. The force applied to the spring then moves the spring tab. The distance the spring tab moves depends on the distance that the aileron is moved.

YOKE MOVEMENT - By turning the yoke right the right aileron moves up and the left aileron moves down.

Anti-servo tabs are located on the back edge of a stabilator. These tabs cause extra drag when the pilot moves the stabilator. Because stabilators can be moved by small control movements, over adjustments would be unavoidable without Anti-servo tabs. The purpose for this extra drag is to keep the pilot from over adjusting the stabilator.

There are three different types of flight controls in an aircraft: primary, secondary and auxiliary. These systems are used together to maneuver and stabilize an aircraft while in flight.
DISCUSSION

Anti-servo tabs automatically change position when the stabilator is adjusted, there is not a separate control for the tabs. Notice how the position of the anti-servo tabs change in respect to the stabilator position.

Most spring controls are adjusted automatically when the associated primary control is adjusted. For example, on some ailerons a spring and push-rod assembly are attached to the aileron and a spring tab.
Knowing how the flight controls are used and how they work is necessary to fully understand the operation of an aircraft. Flight controls are one of the most important systems on an aircraft.
The secondary controls improve performance, stability and relieve excess forces, on the primary controls. Secondary controls include trim tabs and spring tabs.
Flight control systems are used to control the movement and stability of an aircraft while in flight.
